applied.name: Lichtenberg Boulders (granitic boulder field on the north side)

waypoints.name: Stuart Lake Trailhead
waypoints.note: Northwest Forest Pass required for parking; self-issue overnight wilderness permit at the kiosk if camping June 15-Oct 15.

waypoints.name: Colchuck Lake
waypoints.note: Take the left fork staying high on the ridge/shoreline north, avoiding the many spurs that drop to the water.

waypoints.name: Outlet dam creek crossing
waypoints.note: Cross the outlet creek at or just below the small dam on the lake's north end, then pick up the climbers' path on the far side, south for about 100 yards.

waypoints.name: 3rd/4th class rock step
waypoints.note: Short step of rock above a talus clearing; pull up on tree roots and branches with the rock face on your left rather than climbing it head-on.

waypoints.name: Boulder camp in the flats
waypoints.note: Low-impact camping on rock and gravel among boulders just below the col; no reliable water at this camp.

waypoints.name: Colchuck Balanced Rock Col
waypoints.note: Well-cairned path through open forest/hillside (~1 hr from the dam) gains the col; reaching the true summit block from here requires additional 4th/5th-class scrambling.

waypoints.name: Ingalls Creek Trailhead (Trail #1215)
waypoints.note: Off Hwy 97 near Blewett Pass.

waypoints.name: Crystal Creek Junction
waypoints.note: Leave Ingalls Creek Trail ~100 ft before it crosses Crystal Creek.

waypoints.name: Crystal Lake
waypoints.note: Basin camp below the SW Rib; also reachable descending from the Enchantments plateau.

waypoints.name: Crystal Lake Tower
waypoints.note: Westernmost point on McClellan Peak's summit ridge; SW Rib forms a continuous ~1,400-ft line down into Crystal Creek Basin.

waypoints.name: Harlequin Bridge / Campground shuttle stop
waypoints.note: NPS shuttle stop where Stehekin Valley Road crosses the Stehekin River; start of the Stehekin River Trail approach toward Weaver Point.
waypoints.directions: There is no road into Stehekin. Drive to Fields Point Landing or Chelan and take the Lady of the Lake II or Lady Express up-lake — two to four hours depending on which boat — then ride the National Park Service shuttle up the Stehekin Valley Road to the Harlequin Bridge stop. Some parties bike or walk the road instead. Sailings drop to a few a week outside peak summer, so build the trip around the boat schedule rather than the other way round.

waypoints.name: Stehekin River Trail / Devore Creek Trail junction
waypoints.note: Leave the flat Stehekin River Trail here and turn onto Devore Creek Trail #1244, which climbs steeply through rock bluffs into the Glacier Peak Wilderness.
waypoints.directions: Cross Harlequin Bridge at the end of the airstrip and pick up the Stehekin River Trail on the far bank, heading downvalley. It is three essentially flat miles along the river to the junction, which sits about half a mile short of Weaver Point — parties who come in by water taxi to Weaver Point instead join this point from the other direction.

waypoints.name: Bird Creek Camp
waypoints.note: Small established bivy/camp used as base for Devore and Tupshin climbs; reliable water from Bird Creek nearby, last easy flat tent sites before the open basin.
waypoints.directions: Turn uphill and climb hard: roughly 30 switchbacks in about two miles carry the trail through rock bluffs and open forest to the Wilderness boundary near 2,300 ft, and the grade stays relentless for another three-plus miles alongside Devore Creek. The tread through here sees little maintenance and is brushy underfoot. The creek is crossed and paralleled repeatedly and is the water source for the whole stretch.

waypoints.name: Upper Bird Creek basin (~7,000 ft)
waypoints.note: Open basin with small lakes below Devore; cross Bird Creek near the northern lake and head southeast toward the bench/gully leading to Devore's ridge.
waypoints.directions: Leave the maintained trail and follow use paths and animal trails up along Bird Creek, gaining about a mile to an unofficial bench camp near 5,400 ft — parties wanting one big summit day often push to there instead. Gaining a hundred feet or so of hillside before sidehilling keeps the brush manageable; fighting up the creekbed does not. Above the bench the ground steepens into heather benches and a talus staircase, then a second looser gully of scree and dirt, before opening into the lake basin.

waypoints.name: Saddle west of Point 7657
waypoints.note: Col on Devore's southeast ridge reached via a snowfield/talus scramble from the basin; from here the route works west and traverses onto the peak's southeast face.
waypoints.directions: Cross Bird Creek near the northern lake and climb loose Class 2-3 talus and scree southeast out of the basin to the col. Snow lingers here well into July and can leave a short traverse of around 40 degrees, so carry an axe and take crampons if it is likely to be firm. Loose rock and old avalanche debris are the other hazards on this stretch.

waypoints.name: Exposed traverse below summit block
waypoints.note: Class 3-4 ledge traverse across the southeast face to the summit ridge; reported as "extremely exposed 3rd class (4th?)" by climbers and the crux of the descent (reverse or short rappel).
waypoints.directions: From the col, scramble west along the ridge crest, passing the pair of rock towers known locally as the Bottles. The crest then pushes you out onto the southeast face where it steepens and the ledge line begins. Rock quality is mixed — some of it solid, some of it slab under a layer of gravel.

waypoints.name: Devore Peak summit
waypoints.note: True summit at 8,383 ft on the long north-south ridge dividing Company/Hilgard Creek from Devore Creek; summit block requires a short downclimb or rappel on descent.
waypoints.directions: Once across the traverse, scramble easier Class 2-3 ground up an obvious gully to the edge of the summit ridge. The last obstacle is a short, unavoidable rock face of about 20 ft, vertical and exposed. It is the one move on the route that most parties choose to rappel on the way down rather than downclimb.

waypoints.name: Smith Brook Road (FR 6700) — first major switchback, start of the Lichtenwasser Lake approach
waypoints.directions: In summer, drive US 2 to the Smith Brook Road turnoff, Forest Road 6700, roughly 3.5 to 4 miles east of Stevens Pass around mileposts 68.7 to 68.9. Follow the unpaved road up toward the Smithbrook Trailhead and park at or near the first major switchback, where the Lichtenwasser Lake fishing trail leads off toward the lake. In winter FR 6700 is unplowed, so park on the shoulder of US 2 at or just before the Smith Brook Road turnoff and skin or snowshoe 2 to 2.6 miles up the snow-covered road, which is usually well packed by other parties. Start early on a winter trip so the road approach is behind you before the snow softens.

waypoints.name: Lichtenwasser Lake — camp and the launching point for the 248-degree bearing to the saddle
Lichtenberg Boulders (granitic boulder field on the north side)
Phelps Creek Trailhead
waypoints.note: End of Phelps Creek Rd/FR 6211 off Chiwawa River Road; no parking pass or day-use fee required (per USFS), wilderness boundary is 2.6 mi up-trail.
waypoints.directions: From Leavenworth, take US-2 west about 15 miles to Coles Corner, WA-207 north about 4.4 miles, then the Chiwawa Loop Road onto Chiwawa River Road (FR 6200) for roughly 22 miles and FR 6211 for the last 2.3 miles to the trailhead at about 3,500 ft. The gravel and dirt beyond about mile 11 is rough and rutted and is not suitable for low-clearance vehicles; the road is normally snowed shut from late fall through spring and is also subject to washout closures, so check Wenatchee River Ranger District alerts before driving. No parking pass or day-use fee is required, but fill out the free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit at the trailhead.

waypoints.name: Leroy Basin camp
waypoints.note: Established sites reached via a steep unmaintained path off the Leroy Creek crossing (~3.5 mi up Phelps Creek Trail then about 1.5 mi up-basin); streams provide water and there are views of Seven-Fingered Jack.
waypoints.directions: Follow Phelps Creek Trail #1511 up the east side of the valley, a gentle well-graded grade of roughly 275 ft per mile, crossing the wilderness boundary at 2.6 miles and reaching the Leroy Creek ford at about 3.5 miles. Immediately across the ford the unmaintained Leroy Creek high route (#1512) branches steeply up to the north-east; it is well trodden but climbs at roughly 1,200 ft per mile for the final mile and a half into the basin. This half is hot and exposed under a full overnight pack, so carry several liters, and note that campfires are prohibited above 5,000 ft anywhere in the wilderness.

waypoints.name: Leroy Pass
waypoints.note: Sheepherder trail on the Leroy/Carne high route crests here before the cross-country traverse toward Freezer Pass.
waypoints.directions: From camp pick up the Carne Mountain high trail, an old sheepherder track, and follow it south-east; it gives up a little elevation to cross the south fork of Leroy Creek before climbing to the 6,850 ft saddle. Cairns mark the way, but several paths braid apart in the basin, so stay on the lower and better-trodden line where they diverge. About 1.5 miles and roughly 750 ft of net gain from camp.

waypoints.name: Freezer Pass
waypoints.note: Faint footpaths through heather, talus and scree cross the pass and drop cross-country into the Ice Lakes basin.
waypoints.directions: Continue east from the saddle on faint footpaths through heather and then talus and scree, gaining about 750 ft over roughly a mile to the 7,600 ft pass. There is no maintained tread here and the bootpaths come and go, so keep track of your line for the return. Snow can linger on this stretch into early or mid July.

waypoints.name: Lower Ice Lake / old Ice Lakes Trail remnants
waypoints.note: Faint remnants of the historic Ice Lakes Trail mark the point where the route leaves the lakeshore and begins the exposed east traverse toward the Buttes; both lakes are reliable water sources.
waypoints.directions: Drop north-east off the pass down talus into the Ice Lakes basin, losing about 1,000 ft. Pass the north end of Upper Ice Lake and follow the dry stream bed down to the west shore of Lower Ice Lake, then pick up the faint remnants of the old Ice Lakes Trail on the north side. Both lakes are reliable water.

waypoints.name: Creek washout crossing
waypoints.note: Loose, slippery scrub-and-rock traverse around 6,600 ft crosses a hardpan-dirt gully/washout — pick the crossing line carefully, it's easy to end up cliffed out.
waypoints.directions: Leave the lakeshore where the old trail remnants fade and sidehill east at about 6,600 ft, alternating between slippery scrub and loose rock with no real tread. Keep the party strung out in a line rather than stacked one above another, because almost everything here moves underfoot. Roughly a third of a mile brings you to the lip of the washed-out gully.

waypoints.name: Base of the southwest ridge
waypoints.note: Cross-country basin floor between the two Buttes where a scree ramp gains the southwest ridge crest; Class 3 scrambling begins about 400 ft above here, staying climber's right past several loose gendarmes.
waypoints.directions: Pick a crossing line carefully and downclimb the loose clay and scree into the washout, then climb the far side back to about the same elevation; dropping too low here can leave you cliffed out. This is the last reliable water before the summit, so fill up at the crossing. Beyond it the traverse eases and flattens into the open basin floor between the two Buttes, about a third of a mile in all.

waypoints.name: South Spectacle Butte summit
waypoints.note: True summit gained via ledges on the southeast corner of the summit block above ~8,100 ft, after sustained, exposed Class 3 scrambling on the ridge below.
waypoints.directions: From the basin floor climb the scree-and-talus ramp about 400 ft to gain the crest of the southwest ridge, then follow the crest on Class 2-3 talus and broken rock, turning the gendarmes on climber's right. At around 7,700 ft a spire forces the crux: a short chossy chute, a traverse on down-sloping rock, and a Class 3 dike back up, all with real exposure on rotten holds, so move one at a time. Above about 8,100 ft leave the crest for ledges on the south-east corner of the summit block; cairns mark the line but blend into the surrounding rock and are easy to lose.
